summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland operates by self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality can change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar, with no surgery and no court proceeding. In the first months of the route about 350 people had used it.

Same-sex marriage has been in force since 1 July 2022 under the 'Marriage for All' reform, which also opened adoption and IVF to same-sex couples; the reform was approved by 64.1% of voters in referendum.

Public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been punishable under Article 261bis of the Criminal Code since 1 July 2020. That provision does not cover gender identity, so a person targeted specifically for being trans does not receive the criminal-law aggravation available on sexual-orientation grounds. The Criminal Code contains no general hate-crime provision; offences are addressed through the anti-discrimination provisions instead.

Recorded anti-LGBTIQ+ violence is rising. Monitoring by the LGBTIQ Helpline reports roughly six hate crimes per week, 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. OSCE/ODIHR's 2024 Hate Crime Report records that Swiss police do not record bias motivation and that national recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes, so official statistics understate the picture.

On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan to combat hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons, covering 2026 to 2030. Its three pillars are support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence, with the Federal Office for Gender Equality coordinating implementation.

Non-discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is recognised in Swiss law, and same-sex couples have been able to marry since 1 July 2022.

Placement of transgender detainees is governed cantonally rather than nationally. The canton of Basel-Stadt's detention law, adopted by the Grand Council on 13 November 2019, requires separation of female and male detainees and states that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, with the prison directorate permitted to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. No federal trans-prisoner placement rule is recorded and no Swiss case law on the question is recorded; placement practice varies by canton.
tangentialFactors:
ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map maintains an overall index score for Switzerland with a per-category compliance breakdown, reflecting the 2021 self-determination and discrimination votes; the inventory supplies the existence of the rating but not the score itself.

The gap between the statutory position and recorded practice is the main turbulence signal: sexual-orientation offences carry a criminal-law aggravation under Article 261bis while gender-identity-motivated offences do not, and police forces do not code bias motivation, leaving victims dependent on civil-society helpline monitoring for evidence of the scale of attacks.

The fivefold increase in reported cases since 2020 coincides with the period in which legal recognition and marriage reform were adopted, so higher reporting figures reflect both improved willingness to report and a genuinely worsening recorded picture; the sources do not separate the two effects.
localsOnly:
Employers must protect employees' personal dignity under Articles 328 and following of the Code of Obligations, a duty concretised for trans people by the Equality Act (GLG). Trans staff may use their preferred name and gender at work without any change to their official documents.

Implementation of the National Action Plan to combat hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons 2026-2030 is coordinated by the Federal Office for Gender Equality, the federal body also responsible for the overview of LGBTIQ rights.

Detainees in Basel-Stadt are covered by the 2019 JVG separation rules, under which the prison directorate can depart from the male/female separation requirement in consultation with the authority that referred the person, which gives a formal route for placing a trans detainee according to gender identity.

Residents benefit from the general right to equal treatment, with discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity prohibited.
outOfScopeNotes:
The numeric value of the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map index for Switzerland is not present in the inventory and is therefore not stated here.

No federal rule governing the placement of trans prisoners is recorded, nor is any Swiss case law, specialised trans units in places of detention, or federal practice on solitary confinement for trans prisoners; whether such material exists elsewhere is unresolved.

Entry and visa rules, border or airport document screening, gender markers on passports and other identity documents, access to gender-affirming healthcare, and rules on access to sex-segregated facilities such as bathrooms are not addressed by the sources supplied and remain unsourced for this record.

The hate-crime figures derive from LGBTIQ Helpline monitoring rather than police statistics, and official police recording does not code bias motivation, so the relationship between the two data sets is unresolved.
